issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
David, a 65-year-old African American man, sought help for persistent distress stemming from a hurricane that struck his city three years ago. He had been working his shift at a large department store when the storm suddenly intensified. The wind howled, the power flickered and died, and water began to seep in under the main doors. Debris from outside soon blocked the primary exit, trapping David and his colleagues and customers inside. The building creaked and swayed, and for what felt like an eternity, David was certain they would all perish, overcome by a terrifying sense of helplessness as he scanned for any possible escape route that wasn't there.

In the aftermath, David found his memories of the frightening event were like a film that played over and over in his mind. He would often relive the event, feeling vividly like it was happening right now rather than something that was over and done with. As these intrusive memories continued to replay, David started to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that he had permanently changed for the worse, irrevocably altered by the terror he had experienced. This conviction that the world was inherently perilous made him feel he had to be on guard all the time, leading to a pervasive state of hypervigilance where he was constantly superalert and watchful. This belief also kept the traumatic memories feeling disturbingly current and vivid, as if the past danger they represented was still an active threat. His constant state of being on edge, always scanning for potential threats, only served to solidify his belief that the world was indeed a dangerous place and that his vigilance was absolutely necessary for survival.

Convinced that he had to be on guard all the time, David began to implement specific strategies to feel safer. He'd make sure to stay close to the exit in any room or building he entered, and constantly check his surroundings for any signs of danger. His general hypervigilance directly translated into actively scanning for exits as soon as he entered any building, a habit that became second nature. When the memories or anxiety became too intense, David would try to distract himself with something else, though often to little avail.

The intrusive memories continued to exert a powerful pull on David's present experience. When he would relive the event, feeling like it was happening right now, it would immediately trigger a surge of hypervigilance and an intense need to scan for exits. This heightened state of alertness, always on guard, seemed to make his memories of the event more vivid and frequent, creating a distressing feedback loop. At night, this hypervigilance would manifest as severe sleep vigilance; he had great difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, often lying awake for hours, straining to hear every sound. This constant sleep deprivation and hyperarousal only further reinforced his belief that the world was dangerous and that he had permanently changed for the worse, unable to ever truly relax again.

David's coping strategies, while designed to keep him safe, paradoxically tightened the grip of his distress. His constant need to stay near exits and scan his surroundings, particularly in his retail job where he was always interacting with the public in a large, open space, only reinforced his belief that the world was a dangerous place and that he had permanently changed for the worse, needing these elaborate precautions. Actively checking surroundings and scanning for exits kept him in a state of heightened arousal, contributing to his overall hypervigilance and making it almost impossible to relax. His wife, Maria, noticed his increasing preoccupation, his constant scanning of their home, and his difficulty being fully present in conversations. He was exhausted, irritable, and withdrawn, often snapping at her due to his sleep deprivation and persistent anxiety.

The escalating cycle of fear and avoidance eventually brought David to seek help. He was tired of feeling like a prisoner in his own life, constantly on edge, and deeply afraid that he would never feel safe again, forever condemned to a world he perceived as hostile and unpredictable.
